title: Read a simplified text against its original
statement: Check a simplified text by reading it against its original, because a better reading-level score can hide a changed meaning, lost key terms and mechanical prose.
example: Simplified versions read at a lower grade in 68 of 71 pairs, yet one sentence split re-paired ideas and changed a paragraph's meaning.
detail: In a readability trial, a prompted model simplified articles, and the simplified version had a lower reading grade than the original in 68 of 71 rows, for example 16.1 to 11.9 (`icloud-work/k_12_social_studies/ap_files/Articles Tracker.xlsx`, sheet 'ReadabilityExperiment-dev-inter'). Reading the pairs line by line found a sentence split that paired the wrong ideas and changed a paragraph's meaning (cell N13), and splits that gave the prose a predictable, mechanical pattern (cell N8). Review of another simplified run found curriculum terms replaced by everyday words and asked for them to stay (sheet 'APUSH Articles-readable-exp', cell M2).
against: The simplified version was still preferred in most pairs (sheet 'ReadabilityExperiment-dev-inter', column K 'final preference': 23 'New' against 7 'Old', with 41 left blank), so on balance simplifying helped.

evidence.quote: Some of these changes give the flow an overly predictable pattern. That's not always a bad thing, but it can feel very mechanical and repetitive, which is not ideal.
Part 4 is especially concrete: its specified “squared his shoulders” evidence becomes “stood up tall” on the first read and the later model source.
